articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Question: Where the Tourist Tax Actually Goes
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending records shows more than half went to debt service on projects most visitors will never see.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.3 million in tourist development tax revenue in fiscal year 2025, a record high driven by increased hotel rates and occupancy.

More than $25 million—54 percent of collections—went to debt service on the Pensacola Bay Center and other capital projects, with only $8.2 million directed to beach renourishment and tourism marketing combined.
State law gives counties broad discretion over bed tax spending, but critics argue the current allocation prioritizes legacy debt over visitor-facing infrastructure.
articles.body:
The receipt sits in a drawer at the Hampton Inn on Pensacola Beach. A family of four from Birmingham paid $289 for one night in March, plus $14.45 in tourist development tax. They spent the day at the beach, ate grouper tacos on Via de Luna, and left the next morning.

That $14.45 joined $47.3 million collected countywide last fiscal year. Where it went tells a story about how Escambia County has chosen to define tourism infrastructure—and who that definition serves.

Following the Money

The Flightline reviewed five years of Tourist Development Council allocations, county budget documents and bond payment schedules to trace how bed tax revenue flows from hotel rooms to county coffers to final expenditure.

The picture that emerges: a system designed decades ago to fund beach and tourism projects that now functions primarily as a debt service vehicle for downtown facilities.

In fiscal year 2025, the county allocated tourist tax revenue as follows:

  • Pensacola Bay Center debt service: $18.7 million (39.5%)
  • Other capital debt service: $6.8 million (14.4%)
  • Beach renourishment reserves: $5.1 million (10.8%)
  • Visit Pensacola marketing contract: $3.1 million (6.6%)
  • Sports facility grants and maintenance: $4.2 million (8.9%)
  • Administrative costs and reserves: $9.4 million (19.8%)

The Pensacola Bay Center—the downtown arena that hosts Pensacola Ice Flyers games, concerts and conventions—consumes the largest single share. The county issued $95 million in bonds to build the facility in 2017, with tourist tax revenue pledged as the primary repayment source.

What the Law Allows

Florida Statute 125.0104 authorizes counties to levy up to 6 percent in tourist development taxes on short-term rentals. Escambia County levies the full amount. The law specifies nine categories of permitted uses, including beach improvement, tourism promotion and publicly owned convention centers or sports facilities.

The county operates within legal boundaries. The question is whether those boundaries produce outcomes that serve tourists or simply service debt.

"The statute gives us flexibility, and we've used that flexibility," said Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno at a May budget workshop. "Whether you agree with past decisions or not, they were made legally and they have to be honored."

The past decisions he referenced include not just the Bay Center but also the Community Maritime Park bonds, portions of which are backed by tourist tax revenue, and infrastructure improvements at the Pensacola Sports Complex off Langley Avenue.

The Beach Question

Pensacola Beach generates an estimated 60 percent of the county's tourist tax collections, according to Santa Rosa Island Authority figures. The beach falls within Escambia County's tax jurisdiction even though it operates under a separate governance structure through the SRIA.

Beach renourishment—pumping sand onto eroding shorelines—costs roughly $20 million per project and needs to occur every seven to ten years. The current reserve balance of $12.3 million would cover about half of the next scheduled project in 2028.

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio has repeatedly requested increased allocations at Tourist Development Council meetings.

"The visitors come for the beach," Ghio said at the April TDC meeting. "The beach is eroding. The math isn't complicated."

TDC Chair Collier Merrill, who also chairs the county commission, responded that debt obligations limit flexibility.

"We'd all love to put more toward the beach," Merrill said. "But we signed contracts. We made commitments. Those don't disappear because we'd prefer different priorities."

Comparable Counties

A review of tourist tax allocations in Bay County, home to Panama City Beach, and Okaloosa County, which includes Destin and Fort Walton Beach, shows different approaches.

Bay County dedicates 35 percent of its tourist tax revenue to beach renourishment and maintenance, compared to Escambia's 10.8 percent. Okaloosa allocates 28 percent to beach projects and caps debt service obligations at 30 percent of annual collections.

Both counties have lower total collections than Escambia—Bay County brought in $38 million last fiscal year, Okaloosa $41 million—but direct more raw dollars to beach infrastructure.

"Different counties made different choices about what to build and how to pay for it," said Dr. Rick Harper, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies regional tourism. "Escambia went big on an arena. That's neither right nor wrong, but it has a twenty-year tail."

The Utilization Argument

County officials defend the Bay Center investment by pointing to utilization data. The facility hosted 147 events last fiscal year drawing 412,000 attendees, according to SMG, the management company.

"Those are heads in beds," said Visit Pensacola President Darien Schaefer. "A concert brings people from Mobile, from Tallahassee. They stay in our hotels. They pay the tax. It's circular."

But a 2024 economic impact study commissioned by the county found that only 23 percent of Bay Center attendees came from outside a 50-mile radius. Local residents attending Ice Flyers games don't generate hotel stays.

The same study estimated the facility produces $31 million in annual economic impact—a figure that includes spending at nearby restaurants and bars but doesn't account for the $18.7 million in annual debt service.

What Visitors See

The family from Birmingham didn't visit the Pensacola Bay Center. They didn't know it existed. Their $14.45 contribution to the tourist tax will help pay for it anyway.

This isn't unusual. Tourist taxes fund facilities locals use. Hotel guests pay for convention centers they'll never enter. The premise is that these facilities attract future visitors who will spend money that benefits everyone.

Whether that premise holds depends on what you measure and how long you wait to measure it.

The Bay Center bonds mature in 2042. Beach erosion doesn't wait for bond schedules.

What Happens Next

The Tourist Development Council meets June 19 to begin discussing fiscal year 2027 allocations. Ghio has submitted a formal request to increase beach funding to 15 percent of collections. Visit Pensacola has requested a 12 percent increase in its marketing contract.

Both requests exceed available revenue under current debt obligations.

The county could refinance the Bay Center bonds at current rates, which are lower than the original 2017 issuance, potentially freeing $2-3 million annually. County staff have not formally proposed this option.

The county could also increase the bed tax rate, but Escambia already levies the maximum allowed under state law. Increasing it would require legislative action in Tallahassee.

For now, the constraints are fixed. The choices within them are not.

The TDC meeting is scheduled for 9 a.m. at the County Administrative Complex, 3363 West Park Place. Public comment will be accepted.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Last Vacant Lot on Palafox
articles.dek: A 0.3-acre patch of dirt at Palafox and Gregory has sat empty for six years while downtown boomed around it. Three owners, two failed projects, and one stubborn zoning dispute explain why.
brief: The 0.3-acre lot at Palafox and Gregory streets has remained vacant since 2020 despite downtown Pensacola's development surge
Three ownership changes and two abandoned projects have left the property in limbo, complicated by a zoning dispute over building height restrictions
Current owner Coastal Development Partners says a resolution with the city could come by fall 2026, but neighbors remain skeptical
articles.body:
The chain-link fence sags at the corner where teenagers cut through on Friday nights. Inside, sand spurs and bahia grass have colonized the cracked asphalt where a Texaco station stood until 2018. A sun-bleached real estate sign advertises a phone number that now belongs to a seafood restaurant in Mobile.

This is 401 South Palafox Street. One-third of an acre. The last vacant lot on Pensacola's main commercial corridor.

Walk two blocks north and you hit the Bowden Building, its ground-floor retail fully leased. One block south sits the completed first phase of The Standard, 142 apartments that filled within four months of opening. Across Gregory Street, construction crews are finishing a five-story mixed-use project that broke ground eighteen months ago.

But here, at what urban planners once called the most developable corner in downtown Pensacola, nothing has risen from the dirt in six years.

Three owners, no shovels

The lot's modern vacancy began in January 2020 when the Texaco closed after forty-three years. Environmental remediation took fourteen months. Escambia County property records show the site sold in March 2021 to Palafox Corner LLC, a Georgia-based investment group, for $1.2 million.

Palafox Corner announced plans for a six-story boutique hotel. Renderings showed a rooftop bar with bay views. The Pensacola Downtown Improvement Board featured the project in its 2021 annual report.

By October 2022, Palafox Corner had filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. The lot went to auction.

The second buyer was Gregory Street Partners, a Pensacola LLC registered to local attorney Marcus Webb. Webb told the Pensacola News Journal in December 2022 that he planned a three-story mixed-use building with retail on the ground floor and eight residential units above.

"Something modest that fits the neighborhood," Webb said at the time.

Gregory Street Partners held the property for eleven months before selling to the current owner, Coastal Development Partners, in November 2023. Webb did not respond to three phone calls and two emails requesting comment for this article.

Escambia County records show the sale price was $1.8 million—a fifty percent increase from the 2021 purchase despite no improvements to the site.

The height problem

Coastal Development Partners is a Jacksonville-based firm with projects in St. Augustine, Fernandina Beach, and Panama City. Managing partner Elena Castillo said in a phone interview that the company knew about the lot's complications before purchasing.

"We specialize in difficult urban sites," Castillo said. "This one has a specific issue that previous owners either didn't understand or didn't want to fight."

The issue is building height.

The lot sits within the Palafox Commercial District, which allows structures up to seventy-five feet under Pensacola's Land Development Code. But it also falls within a secondary overlay zone—the Gregory Street Historic Transition Area—established in 2019 to protect sightlines to the Saenger Theatre two blocks west.

That overlay caps building height at forty-five feet.

For a developer, the thirty-foot difference means losing two rentable floors. On a 0.3-acre lot in downtown Pensacola, Castillo said, that changes the math from profitable to marginal.

"You can build a three-story building there," Castillo said. "But with current construction costs and land prices, you can't make the numbers work on three stories. You need five."

The overlay zone was the work of the North Hill Preservation Association, which successfully lobbied Pensacola City Council to adopt the height restrictions seven years ago. Association president Dorothy Harmon said the rule exists for good reason.

"Gregory Street is the seam between the commercial district and the historic neighborhoods," Harmon said. "You start allowing seventy-five-foot buildings there, you've changed the character of North Hill forever."

Harmon said her organization would oppose any variance request from Coastal Development Partners.

A variance, or a fight

Castillo said her company has not yet applied for a height variance. She described ongoing "informal conversations" with city planning staff about potential compromises—a stepped-back upper floor, enhanced streetscape improvements, or a historic preservation contribution in exchange for additional height.

"We think there's a path to something everyone can live with," Castillo said. "We're not trying to build a tower. We're asking for fifty-five feet instead of forty-five."

Pensacola Planning Director James Thornton declined to discuss specific conversations with Coastal Development Partners, citing the informal nature of the talks. He confirmed that any height variance would require approval from the city's Board of Zoning Adjustment, with appeals possible to City Council.

"The process is the process," Thornton said. "We can't pre-judge an application that hasn't been filed."

City Council member Allison Chen, whose District 6 includes the lot, said she has received calls from both sides.

"I understand the frustration," Chen said. "People want to see something built there. But the height restrictions exist for a reason, and I'm not going to prejudge a variance application before I see what they're actually proposing."

Meanwhile, sand spurs

On a Tuesday afternoon in late May, the lot at Palafox and Gregory looked much as it has for six years. A paper coffee cup had blown against the fence. The real estate sign leaned fifteen degrees off vertical. Two mockingbirds worked the grass for insects.

Across the street, Tommy Chen—no relation to the council member—swept the sidewalk outside his dry cleaning business. He has watched the lot sit empty since the Texaco closed.

"Every few months somebody comes out, takes pictures, measures stuff," Chen said. "Then nothing. I'll believe it when I see a crane."

Castillo said Coastal Development Partners expects to file a formal variance application by late summer, with a Board of Zoning Adjustment hearing possible in October or November. If approved, construction could begin in spring 2027.

If denied, she said, the company would evaluate its options. Selling the lot is one of them.

"We're patient," Castillo said. "But we're not infinitely patient."

The lot, presumably, can wait as long as it needs to.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Begins With New Flight Path Over Gulf Breeze
articles.dek: Noise complaints from Pensacola Beach residents prompted a route change for this year's practice sessions. Some Gulf Breeze neighbors say they weren't consulted.
brief: Blue Angels practice flights for 2026 Homecoming now route over Gulf Breeze's Tiger Point and Midway areas instead of Pensacola Beach
Naval Air Station Pensacola officials say the change responds to noise complaints filed by Pensacola Beach residents over the past two years
Gulf Breeze residents along the new corridor say they learned of the route change only when jets flew overhead Tuesday morning
articles.body:
The first Blue Angels F/A-18 Super Hornet screamed over Indian Bayou at 9:47 a.m. Tuesday. Karen Whitfield was in her backyard in Tiger Point, watering tomato plants. She dropped the hose.

"I thought something had exploded," Whitfield said. "I've lived here 22 years. They've never come over us like that."

The Navy's elite flight demonstration squadron began practice sessions this week ahead of the annual Homecoming Air Show, scheduled for Nov. 6-7 at Naval Air Station Pensacola. For the first time in the event's modern history, the team is flying a modified route that shifts portions of their practice pattern from Pensacola Beach to the Tiger Point and Midway neighborhoods of Gulf Breeze.

Naval Air Station Pensacola confirmed the change in a statement Thursday, attributing it to "community feedback" gathered over the past two years.

"The Navy takes its responsibility to be a good neighbor seriously," the statement read. "After reviewing concerns raised by residents of Pensacola Beach regarding noise levels during practice sessions, we worked with the Blue Angels to identify an adjusted flight corridor that maintains operational requirements while distributing impact across a wider area."

The statement did not specify how many complaints the base received or through what channels.

No advance notice, residents say

Gulf Breeze Mayor Scott Peaden said he learned of the route change the same way Whitfield did—when the jets flew over.

"I got a call from the base after the fact, Tuesday afternoon," Peaden said. "They were apologetic about the communication breakdown. But the decision had already been made."

Peaden said he requested a meeting with NAS Pensacola leadership to discuss the process. That meeting is tentatively scheduled for next week.

Residents along the new flight path—roughly from the Pensacola Bay Bridge east to Tiger Point Golf Club and south to Midway—described the first practice session as jarring. Multiple residents said windows rattled and pets panicked.

"My dog hid under the bed for three hours," said Marcus Chen, who lives on Bay Forest Drive. "Look, I'm not anti-military. I moved here knowing the base was there. But a heads-up would have been nice."

The Flightline reviewed flight tracking data and resident accounts to approximate the new corridor. The adjusted route appears to bring jets over more densely populated residential areas than the previous path, which primarily crossed the less developed western portions of Pensacola Beach and Santa Rosa Sound.

Beach residents had complained

Pensacola Beach residents have raised noise concerns about Blue Angels practice flights at Santa Rosa Island Authority meetings dating back to at least 2019, according to meeting minutes reviewed by The Flightline.

Complaints intensified in 2024 after the Blue Angels increased practice frequency ahead of their 50th anniversary Homecoming celebration. Some residents cited difficulty working from home, disrupted vacation rentals and concerns about hearing damage for outdoor workers.

The SRIA does not have authority over military flight operations, and Chair Tammy Bohannon repeatedly told residents at the time to direct complaints to the Navy.

"We heard from a lot of folks," Bohannon said Thursday. "This has been a topic at our meetings for years. I can't speak to the Navy's decision, but I understand why beach residents felt they needed to advocate for themselves."

Pensacola Beach resident and vacation rental owner David Marchetti was among those who filed formal complaints with NAS Pensacola through the base's online noise concern form.

"I don't feel great that the problem just got moved to someone else's neighborhood," Marchetti said. "But I also had guests leaving one-star reviews because jets were shaking their rental at 9 a.m. That's a real business impact."

Navy says route balances factors

Lt. Cmdr. Rebecca Torres, public affairs officer for NAS Pensacola, said the new flight path was developed over several months in consultation with Blue Angels leadership and base operations.

Torres said the Navy did not conduct public outreach in Gulf Breeze prior to implementing the change because the new route remains entirely within existing military training airspace.

"These adjustments are operational decisions," Torres said. "We're not required to seek community input for changes within authorized airspace. That said, we recognize this is a transition, and we're committed to being responsive to concerns as they arise."

Torres said residents can submit noise concerns through the NAS Pensacola website. She did not say whether complaints would result in further route modifications.

The Blue Angels are scheduled to practice Tuesday through Thursday this week and next, weather permitting, with shows on Nov. 6 and 7. Practice sessions typically run from 9:30 a.m. to noon, with afternoon sessions possible.

Whitfield, the Tiger Point resident, said she plans to attend the air show as she has most years. She's less sure about the practices.

"I support the Blue Angels. I really do," she said. "I just wish someone had knocked on my door first."
